slides.text: Hannah made her living restoring antique garments in a quiet basement shop off Portobello Road. She believed fabrics retained the emotional memory of those who wore them—salt stains from forgotten tears, smoke from Parisian bistros, perfume trapped in wool fibers. In autumn, she purchased a magnificent charcoal cashmere overcoat tailored in Vienna in 1958. While repairing the silk lining of the inner breast pocket, her shears brushed against something stiff: an unpunched, yellowed sleeper-train ticket from Zurich to Rome.

Tucked inside the ticket was a handwritten note in faded fountain-pen ink: 'If you board the 8:15 to Santa Lucia, I will know you forgive me. If you do not, keep this coat against the winter wind.' The ticket had never been validated; whoever owned the coat had chosen to stay behind. For years, Hannah kept the coat on a cedar mannequin near the shop window, touched by the tragic ghost of an unmade journey she could never mend.

On a freezing December afternoon, an elderly gentleman with kind, silver eyes entered the shop, stopped dead in his tracks before the mannequin, and began to weep. From his wallet, he pulled a brittle, folded paper: the missing ticket stub for the matching seat beside it on the 8:15. 'She did keep it,' the old man whispered, his trembling fingers tracing the lapel. 'Sixty years I wondered if she ever reached the station. She kept me warm all this time.'
